Greetings! Today I woke up and chose to do coinduction in lean. Ive scketched a few things, but I need your help!

  1. In the linked code, can some attribute be slapped onto replicate to silence the nondecreasing argument stuff?
  2. What is the reason for lean to reject seqv_ext_eq?

Your type is empty:

instance {T} : IsEmpty (Seqv T) := by
  refine ⟨fun x ↦ ?_⟩
  induction x with
  | step _ _ ih => exact ih ()
There is no support for coinductive types in Lean yet.

I believe there is some support for coinductive predicates

def Cong {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (r : α → β → Prop) (f : Nat → α) (g : Nat → β) : Prop :=
  r (f 0) (g 0) ∧ Cong r (fun i => f (i + 1)) (fun i => g (i + 1))
coinductive_fixpoint

/--
info: Cong.coinduct.{u, v} {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (r : α → β → Prop) (pred : (Nat → α) → (Nat → β) → Prop)
  (hyp : ∀ (f : Nat → α) (g : Nat → β), pred f g → r (f 0) (g 0) ∧ pred (fun i => f (i + 1)) fun i => g (i + 1))
  (f : Nat → α) (g : Nat → β) : pred f g → Cong r f g
-/
#guard_msgs in
#check Cong.coinduct

you can also write it like this

coinductive Cong {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (r : α → β → Prop) :
    (f : Nat → α) → (g : Nat → β) → Prop where
  | intro {f : Nat → α} {g : Nat → β} (x : r (f 0) (g 0))
    (xs : Cong r (fun i => f (i + 1)) (fun i => g (i + 1))) : Cong r f g

/--
info: Cong.coinduct.{u, v} {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (r : α → β → Prop) (pred : (Nat → α) → (Nat → β) → Prop)
  (hyp : ∀ (f : Nat → α) (g : Nat → β), pred f g → r (f 0) (g 0) ∧ pred (fun i => f (i + 1)) fun i => g (i + 1))
  (f : Nat → α) (g : Nat → β) : pred f g → Cong r f g
-/
#guard_msgs in
#check Cong.coinduct

See for example this old discussion and https://github.com/alexkeizer/QPFTypes by @Alex Keizer but note the readme says "It is still very rough, and not at all ready for serious use."

This looks like just an (infinite) stream type? For that, the QPFTypes library should work, although one reason for that warning is also that there's no support for elaborating corecursive functions yet, so you'll have to write functions directly in terms of the corecursion principle

deepest recursion schrieb:

Well, this is bizarre, because I don't see how it can be a valid statement. I am also failing to comprehend what justifies the presence of ih, it feels somewhat bogus.

Well the whole point of inductive (as opposed to what would be coinductive) is that you can entirely recurse through an element of the type, i.e. that this is allowed:

inductive Seqv (T) where
  | step (item:T) (next: Unit -> (Seqv T))

def Seqv.false (x : Seqv T) : False :=
  match x with
  | .step item next =>
    Seqv.false (next ())

This would not be true of coinductive (if we had coinductive) but this is natural for inductive.

I recently wrote a library for defining coinductive types based on basically the same idea as QPFTypes: https://github.com/ISTA-PLV/coinductive

The key feature of the library is that it allows one to define recursive functions on coinductive types using the partial fixpoint command (see for example Test/Stream.lean in the repo):

def Stream.map (f : α → β) (s : Stream α) : Stream β :=
  match s.unfold with
  | .snil        => .snil
  | .scons hd tl => .scons (f hd) (Stream.map f tl)
partial_fixpoint

The library is still very young, not much battle tested, and might change in the future, but the definition of coinductive types is quite simple so I hope that it will be relatively stable. (No guarantees though.)

Cool to see other people working in this space too! Does this definition actually have the right logical meaning, though? I'd thought about using partial_fixpoint, but I was under the impression it would map all infinite computations to a single fallback "divergence" element

That is, looking at that example

def s3 : Stream Nat :=
  .scons 0 $ .scons 1 $ .stail s3
partial_fixpoint

Is it provable that the head of s3 is 0?

Yes

theorem s3_head :
  Stream.shead s3 = some 0 := by
    unfold s3
    simp [Stream.shead]

(partial_fixpoint provides an equality that s3 is equal to .scons 0 $ .scons 1 $ .stail s3, which is sufficient to prove this property.)
This is all based on a custom CCPO structure for coinductive types, not using the flat order. See here for the partial order that defines the CCPO.

One limitation is that this stream type has a snil constructor (i.e. streams are finite or infinite). This is necessary to have a nice bottom element for the CCPO structure. If one defines Stream without snil it is not clear to me how to pick the bottom element of the CCPO structure such that one can prove that Stream.map is monotonic. (This is not a problem for ITrees where one can define the bottom element using tau.)
nice! is it fully universe polymorphic?

Ooh, I hadn't expected that, cool!

Is it perhaps possible to prove that Stream.map always returns an infinite stream (when the argument is infinite), and use that to coerce your definition of Stream.map into a function over truly infinite streams?

I did not test it with complex universes, but it should in principle be universe polymorphic. There is no meta code and all definitions should be universe polymorphic (if I did not make a mistake somewhere). The following works:

def test : Stream PUnit.{2} := .scons ⟨⟩ test
partial_fixpoint

That is an interesting idea. I have not tried it, but maybe it would work.

Michael Sammler said:

That is an interesting idea. I have not tried it, but maybe it would work.

I gave it a try, and indeed this works! Essentially, you can define StreamF to have just the scons constructor, so that Stream := CoInd StreamF is the type of truly infinite streams, and then have (Option <| StreamF .) be the functor in which you have the bottom, and can thus have definitions using partial fixpoint. Then, you can define a coinductive predicate on OptStream := CoInd (Option <| StreamF .) that states a particular possibly finite stream is actually infinite; with this predicate you can then define a function OptStream -> Stream, now you just have to prove that map preserves infinite-ness, and you can lift an OptStream.map definition into a Stream.map.

Next, I tried to #eval a take function that would give the first n elements of one of the streams, and Lean promptly died... On second thought, it makes sense that partial_fixpoint would not magically make the definitions lazy, so I guess that means these infinite definitions are effectively non-computable? That would be a little disappointing. @Michael Sammler is this a known limitation?

I also experimented around with Stream and could not get it to compute well. I think if the recursive occurrence is not under a lambda, Lean will evaluate too eagerly and then it crashes. Not sure if one can fix this somehow.

However, there is also good news: If the recursive occurrence is underneath a lambda, one can actually compute with the coinductive types. Not sure how to do this for Streams since none of its constructors adds a lambda, but this works for ITrees:

def print_inf (n : Nat) : ITree (logE Nat) Empty :=
  do log n; print_inf (n + 1)
partial_fixpoint

/--
info: 0
---
info: 1
---
info: 2
---
info: 3
---
info: 4
---
info: none
-/
#guard_msgs in
#eval evalN (Lean.Elab.Command.CommandElabM) 5 (print_inf 0)

The evalN function here evaluates the ITree up to depth 5.

I've used this to get an interpreter for Iris' Heaplang language (based on the ITree semantics given by Program Logics à la Carte), where one can for example evaluate this concurrent heaplang program (using a fixed round robin scheduler):

/-- info: some (HeapLang.Val.lit (HeapLang.BaseLit.unit)) -/
#guard_msgs in
#eval evalN heaplangM 10000 hl(
  let x := ref(#0);
  fork(x ← (!x + #1));
  x ← (!x + #1);
  assert(!x = #2)).denote

So I played around with it a bit, and you can just replace the second argument of scons with a Unit -> Stream or Thunk Stream:

inductive StreamF (α : Type w) (Stream : Type w) : Type w where
  | snil
  | scons (x : α) (tl : Thunk Stream)

I've not proven all the monotonicity lemmas, but presumably those proofs wouldn't actually break. I have confirmed that this indeed computes reasonably well.

It's not fully transparent, in that it does change the type of the constructor, but it's isomorphic and if it's really problematic could be resolved with similar macro_inline trickery that the standard library uses to ensure laziness for the branches of an if-then-else (ite)

Also, I noticed that the Thunk approach for computing with Stream suffers from severe performance problems and seems to take exponential time. For instance, taking 25 elements from a stream requires 30 seconds to run:

import Coinductive

namespace Stream
open Coinductive Lean.Order

inductive StreamF (α : Type u) (Stream : Type u) : Type u where
| snil
| scons (x : α) (tl : Thunk Stream)

inductive StreamF.In (α : Type u) : Type u where
| snil
| scons (x : α)

@[simp, grind =]
theorem Thunk.get_mk (fn : Unit → α) : Thunk.get ⟨fn⟩ = fn () := by rfl

@[simp]
theorem Thunk.mk_get (x : Thunk α) : Thunk.mk (fun _ ↦ x.get) = x := by simp [Thunk.ext_iff]

instance (α : Type u) : PF (StreamF α)
    where
  P :=
    ⟨StreamF.In α, fun
      | .snil => PEmpty
      | .scons _ => PUnit⟩
  unpack
    | .snil => .obj (.snil) nofun
    | .scons hd tl => .obj (.scons hd) fun _ ↦ tl.get
  pack
    | .obj (.snil) _ => .snil
    | .obj (.scons hd) tl => .scons hd (tl ⟨⟩)
  unpack_pack := by rintro _ (_ | _) <;> simp
  pack_unpack := by rintro _ (⟨⟨⟩, _⟩ | ⟨⟨⟩⟩) <;> simp <;> funext x <;> cases x

abbrev Stream (α : Type u) : Type u :=
  CoInd (StreamF α)

def Stream.fold (t : StreamF α (Stream α)) : Stream α :=
  CoInd.fold _ t

def Stream.snil : Stream α :=
  .fold .snil

def Stream.scons (hd : α) (tl : Thunk (Stream α)) : Stream α :=
  .fold <| .scons hd tl

@[simp]
theorem unfold_snil : CoInd.unfold _ Stream.snil = StreamF.snil (α := α) := by simp [Stream.snil, Stream.fold]

@[simp]
theorem unfold_scons : CoInd.unfold _ (Stream.scons i s) = StreamF.scons i s := by simp [Stream.scons, Stream.fold]

instance : Inhabited (StreamF α PUnit) where default := .snil

@[simp]
theorem Stream.bot_eq : CoInd.bot (StreamF α) = Stream.snil :=
  by
  rw [CoInd.bot_eq]
  simp [PF.map, PF.pack, Stream.snil, Stream.fold]

theorem Stream.le_unfold (s1 s2 : Stream α) :
    (s1 ⊑ s2) = (s1 = .snil ∨ ∃ i s1' s2', s1 = .scons i s1' ∧ s2 = .scons i s2' ∧ s1'.get ⊑ s2'.get) :=
  by
  ext
  constructor
  · intro h
    rw [CoInd.le_unfold] at h
    rcases h with (rfl | ⟨i, _, _, _, _, h1, h2⟩); simp
    rw [← unfold_fold _ s1, ← unfold_fold _ s2]
    rw [← PF.unpack_pack s1.unfold, ← PF.unpack_pack s2.unfold]
    simp only [h1, h2]
    cases i <;> simp [PF.pack, snil, scons, fold]
    right
    exists ?_, ?_; rotate_left 1
    constructor; rfl
    apply Exists.intro
    constructor; rfl
    simp_all
  · rintro (rfl | ⟨_, _, _, rfl, rfl, _⟩)
    · simp [CoInd.le_unfold]
    · simp [CoInd.le_unfold]
      right
      simp [PF.unpack]
      constructor <;> try rfl
      grind

theorem scons_monoN α i (s1 s2 : Thunk (Stream α)) n :
    CoIndN.le _ (s1.get.approx n) (s2.get.approx n) →
      CoIndN.le _ ((Stream.scons i s1).approx (n + 1)) ((Stream.scons i s2).approx (n + 1)) :=
  by
  intro hs
  simp [CoIndN.le, PF.unpack]
  right
  constructor <;> try rfl
  grind [coherent1]

@[partial_fixpoint_monotone]
theorem scons_mono [PartialOrder β] i (f : β → Stream α) : monotone f → monotone fun x ↦ Stream.scons i ⟨fun _ ↦ f x⟩ :=
  by
  intro hf t1 t2 hle
  apply CoInd.le_leN
  rintro ⟨n⟩; simp [CoIndN.le]
  apply scons_monoN
  grind [CoInd.leN_le, monotone]

def Stream.map (f : α → β) (s : Stream α) : Stream β :=
  match s.unfold with
  | .snil => .snil
  | .scons hd tl => .scons (f hd) (Stream.map f tl.get)
partial_fixpoint

@[partial_fixpoint_monotone]
theorem map_mono [PartialOrder γ] (f : α → β) (g : γ → Stream α) : monotone g → monotone fun x ↦ Stream.map f (g x) :=
  by
  intro hf t1 t2 hle
  apply CoInd.le_leN
  intro n
  dsimp only
  have hs : (g t1) ⊑ (g t2) := by grind [monotone]
  generalize g t1 = s1, g t2 = s2 at hs
  induction n generalizing s1 s2 with
  | zero => simp [CoIndN.le]
  | succ n ih =>
    unfold Stream.map
    rw [Stream.le_unfold] at hs
    rcases hs with rfl | ⟨hd, tl1, tl2, rfl, rfl, htl⟩
    · simp [CoIndN.le, CoIndN.bot]
    · simp_all
      simp [CoIndN.le, PF.unpack]
      right
      constructor <;> try rfl
      intro x
      exact ih _ _ htl

def Stream.stail (s : Stream α) : Stream α :=
  match s.unfold with
  | .snil => .snil
  | .scons _ tl => tl.get

@[partial_fixpoint_monotone]
theorem stail_mono [PartialOrder β] (f : β → Stream α) : monotone f → monotone fun x => Stream.stail (f x) :=
  by
  intro hf t1 t2 hle
  apply CoInd.le_leN
  intro n
  dsimp only
  cases n; simp [CoIndN.le]
  have hs : (f t1) ⊑ (f t2) := by grind [monotone]
  generalize f t1 = s1, f t2 = s2 at hs
  unfold Stream.stail
  rw [Stream.le_unfold] at hs
  rcases hs with ⟨_ | _⟩
  · simp [CoIndN.le, CoIndN.bot]
  next h =>
    rcases h with ⟨_, _, _, _, _, _⟩
    simp_all
    grind [CoInd.leN_le]

def Stream.shead (s : Stream α) : Option α :=
  match s.unfold with
  | .snil => none
  | .scons hd _ => some hd

def Stream.take (s : Stream α) : Nat → List (Option α)
  | 0 => []
  | n + 1 => s.shead :: s.stail.take n

def pos :=
  Stream.scons (1 : Rat) <| pos.map (· + 1)
partial_fixpoint

#eval pos.take 10

end Stream

def main :=
  IO.println <| Stream.pos.take 25

Whereas a similar program in Haskell takes linear time to run:

pos = 1 : map (1+) pos
take 2500 pos

This is indeed an interesting observation. It seems like this is due to the use of map. If one defines pos as the following, evaluation is instantaneous: 

def pos (n : Rat) :=
  Stream.scons (n : Rat) <| pos (n + 1)
partial_fixpoint

coinductive OptStream.IsInf : (xs : OptStream α) → Prop where
  | scons (x xs) : OptStream.IsInf xs → OptStream.IsInf (.scons x xs)
